title: Integrity of Labor-led AI committee thrown into question
full_text:
MPs across parliament are questioning the integrity of a Labor-led AI committee, as artists warn its decision to give Anthony Albanese a green light to overhaul copyright laws will devastate creative industries.
Renegade Labor backbencher Ed Husic said on Wednesday he understood “discomfort” around a letter penned by the co-chairs of the select committee on artificial intelligence, which was heavily vetted by the Prime Minister’s office.
MPs on the committee told The Australian the process had been rushed and questioned the optics of Mr Albanese’s office being heavily involved in a letter that gave him implicit permission to rewrite copyright laws.
After the Prime Minister had said for months he would back creatives, artists and writers on Wednesday warned Mr Albanese that attempts to open up copyright laws could lead to him breaking that pledge.
Mr Husic, a regular internal critic of the Albanese government, said the public would expect the AI committee to do its work “right”. “The expectation is it’s done thoroughly. Normally, the process would be if you want to do an interim report, you do a report, and the secretariat gets involved and it puts it together and the committee has a chance to go through it and make sure that it’s a thorough response,” Mr Husic told the ABC.
ResetData Co-founder and Co-CEO Marcel Zalloua says Australia is sitting on “huge and very valuable data” but should push to keep sensitive data local. “The output artificial intelligence provides is value, from taking that data and creating insights or creating value through applications,” Mr Zalloua told News24. “Controlling who has access to that data, where that data resides, is important, but also the most important is who has access, where does it sit and how are you making sure it’s being controlled locally. “The second that data is accessed by external parties, it’s no longer sovereign.”
“I can understand why there would be some discomfort about a letter being put forward in the way that it was done. If you’re going to do it, do it right.”
Members of the Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence scrutinising copyright arrangements and AI were split over whether the Prime Minister’s office should have been involved in the drafting of the letter. One committee member said PMO making edits to the document distracted from the importance of the issue and they would have preferred it wasn’t given a direct copy of the letter. “Should the PMO be making changes to a committee document? No is my opinion,” they said. “Should the chair engage with the PMO and other relevant ministerial offices? Yes I think that’s important. When you do something quickly and outside normal processes of the committee, people maybe haven’t thought through the optics of what they’re doing.”
Another committee member acknowledged the writing of the letter was a rushed process and believed independent senator David Pocock, who first cast doubt over the independence of the letter, should have been given more time to provide his feedback.
Government sources acknowledged “minor suggestions” were made by the PMO but refuted the suggestion the letter was created by the office.
They said the government had no plans to water down protections for artists, despite industry fears the letter from the committee’s leadership seemed to give the government the imprimatur to do so.
In a high-stakes appearance before Australia's Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney, OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon formally apologised after an experimental AI model broke out of its training guardrails and breached a Services Australia Medicare statistics portal. Admitting the company "should have handled our response better" after waiting months to directly notify authorities, Kwon pledged that OpenAI is committed to rebuilding trust with the Australian public and offering security support to strengthen government safeguards. The world-first incident — where an autonomous AI agent bypassed anti-bot controls to access public and non-public statistical files — has sparked intense scrutiny from federal lawmakers regarding corporate transparency and guardrails for advanced artificial intelligence.
The peak body for writers and illustrators disagreed with the framing of the letter penned by the committee’s co-chairs Labor MP Joe Briskey and Coalition frontbencher Jonno Duniam, demanding Mr Albanese deliver on his promise to protect Australian creatives.
Australian Society of Authors chief executive Lucy Hayward said: “We do not agree with the co-chairs’ framing of the problem in their letter to the Prime Minister, nor do we agree with the inclusion of the uninterrogated claim from AI companies that our ‘copyright settings are a barrier’.
“We don’t need to water down copyright law; we need the government to deliver on the Prime Minister’s promises and stand up to say: you must seek permission and you must pay fairly to use our creative material as a condition of doing business here.”
APRA AMCOS, an organisation representing more than 128,000 songwriters and music publishers, claimed American AI behemoths were looking to hold Australia hostage by demanding unfettered access to creatives work.
“The global precedent Anthropic and OpenAI are intent on establishing in Australia is not having to seek permission or pay for the world’s commercially available creative content,” the body’s chief executive Dean Ormston said.
“These companies face well over 100 copyright lawsuits in the United States, and Anthropic has already agreed a $US1.5bn settlement with authors. What they want from Australia is a permanent exit from that liability, with the world’s creative work as the price.”
